Initial Report (filed 2:15 p.m.): Bramwell Motors announced today it is recalling approximately 45,000 units of its 2024-2025 Voltra EV due to a software defect that could cause the parking brake to disengage unexpectedly on inclines steeper than 15 degrees. The company said owners would be notified by mail within two weeks and that a free over-the-air software update would resolve the issue for most vehicles; a small subset built before November 2024 will need an in-person dealer visit to replace a related sensor.

Correction (filed 5:40 p.m.): Bramwell Motors clarified that the recall affects approximately 38,000 units, not 45,000 as the company initially stated in its morning press release; the lower figure excludes about 7,000 vehicles that already received the corrected software during a routine update in March. A company spokesperson said the original figure was based on total production volume rather than the number of affected, unpatched vehicles. All other details of the recall, including the incline threshold and the in-person dealer visit requirement for pre-November 2024 vehicles, remain unchanged.

Separately, rival automaker Halden Auto said its own EV line uses a different parking-brake supplier and is not affected by this recall or any related issue.

Bramwell said no accidents or injuries have been linked to the defect so far, and that the issue was discovered internally during routine validation testing rather than through a customer complaint.

state: A randomized controlled trial examined whether a daily 500mg magnesium supplement reduces the frequency of migraine attacks in adults with episodic migraine. Meta-Analysis: Effect of Structured Exercise Programs on Post-Surgical Recovery Time.

We pooled data from 14 randomized trials (total n=2,340) examining whether structured post-operative exercise programs reduce time to independent mobility after elective hip or knee replacement surgery. Studies varied in exercise intensity, starting point (immediate post-op vs. 1 week post-op), and surgery type.

Pooled results showed that structured exercise programs reduced median time to independent mobility by 1.8 days (95% CI, 1.1-2.5 days) compared to standard care. The effect was larger for knee replacement patients (2.4 days) than hip replacement patients (1.2 days). Programs that began within 24 hours of surgery showed a larger benefit (2.6 days) than those starting after 1 week (0.9 days).

Heterogeneity across studies was moderate (I²=48%), and a funnel plot suggested some possible publication bias, meaning the true pooled effect could be somewhat smaller than reported. Only 3 of the 14 included trials were rated low risk of bias on all domains; the remaining 11 had at least one domain rated as unclear or high risk, most often around blinding of outcome assessors, which is inherently difficult in exercise interventions.

Two trials specifically examining shoulder replacement surgery were excluded from this analysis because shoulder recovery trajectories were judged too clinically different from hip and knee recovery to pool meaningfully; a separate review of shoulder-specific rehabilitation is planned.

No trials included in this analysis reported serious adverse events attributable to the exercise programs themselves, though 4 trials reported temporary increases in reported pain during the first week of the program, which resolved without intervention.

We conclude that structured exercise programs, particularly those started early, are associated with meaningfully faster return to independent mobility after hip or knee replacement, though the moderate heterogeneity and risk-of-bias concerns in most included trials warrant some caution in interpreting the magnitude of this effect.

A pre-specified sensitivity analysis excluding the three trials with the highest risk-of-bias ratings produced a similar pooled estimate (1.6 days, 95% CI 0.9-2.3), suggesting the overall result is not driven solely by lower-quality studies. Subgroup analysis by patient age (above vs. below 70 years) found no statistically significant difference in the size of the exercise benefit between age groups, though the youngest and oldest subgroups had wider confidence intervals due to smaller sample sizes within those strata. Cost data were reported in only 4 of the 14 trials and were not pooled due to substantial differences in how physical therapy visits were billed across health systems; a qualitative summary of those 4 trials suggested structured programs were cost-neutral to modestly cost-saving when accounting for reduced length of hospital stay, but the authors caution this finding is based on a small, non-representative subset of the pooled trials.

state: Erratum to: 'Catalytic Efficiency of Compound X-14 in Nitrogen Fixation' (originally published March 2025). The original article reported a turnover frequency of 420 h⁻¹ for Compound X-14 under standard conditions. Following a re-analysis prompted by an independent lab's inability to replicate this figure, the authors identified a calibration error in the original gas chromatography measurements. The corrected turnover frequency is 168 h⁻¹, roughly 40% of the originally reported value. The authors state that this correction does not affect the paper's qualitative conclusion that Compound X-14 outperforms the previous benchmark catalyst, Compound W-9 (turnover frequency 110 h⁻¹), but does affect the magnitude of the reported improvement, which is now approximately 53% rather than the originally claimed 282%. The authors have also corrected Figure 3 and Table 2 accordingly and thank the independent lab for identifying the discrepancy.

questions.instruction: What was identified as the cause of the original error, according to the erratum?

candidates.description: A calibration error in the gas chromatography measurements
A simple typographical error in the manuscript
A mix-up between Compound X-14 and Compound W-9 samples

questions.notes: Stated directly as a calibration error.

questions.instruction: Which of the following does the erratum support?

candidates.description: The corrected turnover frequency is lower than originally published
Compound X-14 still outperforms Compound W-9 after the correction
The error was attributed to fraud
Figure 3 and Table 2 were left unrevised

questions.notes: 168 < 420 (corrected lower); 168 > 110 (still outperforms W-9); error was calibration, not fraud; figures were corrected.

Visit 1 — March 3: Patient: K. Simmons, presenting with new-onset low back pain after lifting a heavy box, no radiation to legs, no numbness or tingling, no bowel/bladder changes. Exam: tenderness over lumbar paraspinal muscles, normal strength and reflexes, negative straight-leg raise. Assessment: acute lumbar strain. Plan: ibuprofen, heat, gentle stretching, avoid heavy lifting for 2 weeks, return if no improvement in 2 weeks or if red-flag symptoms (numbness, weakness, bowel/bladder changes) develop.

Visit 2 — March 18: Patient returns, reports pain improved about 50% but now notes new tingling radiating down the right leg to the calf over the past 3 days, no bowel/bladder changes, no weakness on exam today. Assessment: findings concerning for possible lumbar disc involvement given new radicular symptoms; strain alone would not typically cause new radiation at this point. Plan: MRI lumbar spine ordered, continue conservative management, referral to physical therapy, follow up after MRI results, return immediately if leg weakness or bowel/bladder changes develop.

Visit 3 — April 2: MRI showed a small L4-L5 disc bulge without significant nerve root compression. Patient reports tingling has since resolved with physical therapy, denies any weakness, denies bowel/bladder changes throughout. Assessment: improving, consistent with mild disc bulge managed conservatively; surgery not indicated at this time. Plan: continue physical therapy for 4 more weeks, taper as tolerated, follow up only if symptoms worsen or new red-flag symptoms appear.

Earnings Call Transcript Excerpt — Vantera Corp Q3 Results.

Operator: We'll now take questions. First question from Ellis Wong at Birchfield Securities.

Ellis Wong: Thanks. Can you talk about the gross margin decline this quarter and whether that's expected to continue?

CFO Rina Alsop: Sure, Ellis. Gross margin was 42%, down from 46% last quarter, primarily due to a one-time inventory write-down of $6 million related to a discontinued product line. Excluding that write-down, gross margin would have been approximately 45.5%, essentially flat sequentially. We don't expect the write-down to recur, so we'd expect margin to normalize back toward the mid-40s next quarter, though component costs remain a modest headwind.

Operator: Next question from Priya Anand at Oakstone Capital.

Priya Anand: On the guidance cut for full-year revenue, how much of that is the divested logistics unit versus organic softness?

CEO Daniel Fenwick: Good question, Priya. Of the $40 million reduction in our full-year guidance, about $30 million reflects the deconsolidation of the logistics unit we sold in August, and the remaining $10 million reflects modestly softer demand in our core enterprise segment, mainly in EMEA. We want to be clear that the divestiture is the larger factor by far.

Priya Anand: Understood. And is the $10 million softness something you expect to persist into next year?

Daniel Fenwick: Too early to say definitively, but the early read from our sales team is that it's more pipeline timing than lost deals, so we're cautiously optimistic it doesn't persist, though we're not baking that optimism into guidance yet.

Operator: Next question from Tomas Reyes at Fielding Asset Management.

Tomas Reyes: Quick one on capital allocation — with the logistics divestiture proceeds, are you planning any share buybacks?

CFO Rina Alsop: Thanks, Tomas. We received $85 million in net proceeds from the divestiture. Our priority is first paying down $25 million of higher-cost debt, and the board has approved a new $50 million buyback authorization for the remainder, though the pace of repurchases will depend on where the stock trades relative to our internal view of intrinsic value. We don't have a specific timeline to share beyond that.

Tomas Reyes: And is that $50 million incremental to the $20 million left on the prior authorization?

CFO Rina Alsop: Good catch — no, the new $50 million authorization replaces and supersedes the prior one; the $20 million remaining under the old authorization is no longer available separately.

Operator: That concludes our Q&A session.

state: Material Restatement Notice: Calloway Foods Inc. announced it will restate its financial statements for fiscal years 2023 and 2024 after identifying an error in how it recognized revenue from long-term co-packing agreements. The company previously recognized revenue upfront upon contract signing; under the correct accounting treatment, revenue should be recognized ratably over the life of each agreement. The restatement is expected to reduce previously reported FY2023 revenue by approximately $14 million and FY2024 revenue by approximately $9 million, with a corresponding increase in revenue recognized in later periods as those contracts continue. The company stated the error does not affect historical cash flows or the total contract value of any agreement, only the timing of when revenue was recognized in the financial statements. The audit committee has concluded the error was unintentional and related to a misapplication of a new accounting standard adopted in early 2023, not to any fraudulent activity. The company's previously issued financial statements for FY2023 and FY2024 should no longer be relied upon.
